find_certificates.description: Scan the newest stretch of a log for certificates covering a domain, optionally including its subdomains. This is how a workflow catches a certificate being issued for a name it owns - the thing Certificate Transparency exists to make visible. Narrow it further by issuing CA, by certificate or precertificate, and by the moment the log accepted it. A log has no search of its own, so this reads entries from the end backwards and filters them here; how far back it looks is up to you, and it says how many it read. No account or API key required.
find_certificates.display_name: Find certificates for a domain in a log
find_certificates.name: find_certificates

parameters.description: Which Certificate Transparency log to read. The dropdown lists the usable and qualified logs with the certificate expiry window each one covers, and stores the log's id rather than its name so a workflow keeps working when a log is renamed. Typed by hand it also takes a log id, a description as the log list writes it, or the log's URL.
parameters.name: log

parameters.description: The domain to look for, such as example.com. Matched against every name on the certificate; a wildcard certificate matches its own parent domain when subdomains are included. A name read off an earlier step works as it comes: a leading '*.' is dropped, since searching for '*.example.com' means the same thing as searching for 'example.com'.
parameters.name: domain

parameters.description: Also match names under the domain, so example.com finds shop.example.com and *.example.com.
parameters.name: include_subdomains

parameters.description: Only certificates whose issuer contains this text, matched without regard to case. Use it to spot a certificate from a CA you do not use.

find_logs_for_expiry.description: Given the day a certificate expires, say which logs could hold it. Certificate Transparency logs are sharded by year - Argon2026h2 only takes certificates expiring in the second half of 2026 - so asking the wrong shard returns nothing, correctly and misleadingly. Pick the expiry date off a certificate and this answers which logs to look in, grouped by operator so a check can be spread across several. No account or API key required.

find_logs_for_expiry.display_str_template: Find the logs that accept certificates expiring {0}.
find_logs_for_expiry.name: find_logs_for_expiry

parameters.description: The day the certificate expires - its 'not after' date. A full timestamp read off an earlier step works too; only the date is used.
parameters.name: expires_on

parameters.description: Only logs in these states. A log's state is what says whether it is worth reading: browsers only trust certificates logged to a usable one, a retired log is frozen, and a rejected one failed qualification and proves nothing. Choose none to see every log.
parameters.name: states

options.label: Usable - trusted, and taking new certificates
Qualified - passed its tests, being included

get_checkpoint.description: Read a tiled log's checkpoint in full: the signed note it publishes in place of a signed tree head, with its origin line, its size, its root hash and every signature on it - including the independent witnesses that co-sign it, which is what makes a tiled log's word harder to take back. Use 'Get a log's tree head' when all that is wanted is the size and the root; use this when the signatures themselves matter. Only tiled logs serve it. No account or API key required.

get_consistency_proof.description: Ask a log to prove that everything it published at an earlier size is still there, unchanged, in the log as it is now. This is the check that makes a transparency log worth the name, and it is what monitoring one looks like: record a tree head's size and root hash today, hand both back tomorrow, and get a yes or a no. Without the earlier root hash the proof is still returned, but nothing can be checked against it. Only RFC 6962 logs serve proofs. No account or API key required.

get_log_list_summary.description: Read which version of the published Certificate Transparency log list is current, when it was published, and what it holds: how many logs there are in each state, how they split between the RFC 6962 and tiled formats, how many operators run them, and the range of certificate expiry dates the logs cover between them. Run it to check for a new version of the list before doing anything else. No account or API key required.

get_tree_head.description: Read how big a log is right now and the root hash that commits to everything in it. This is a log's heartbeat: the tree size says how many certificates it holds, and the root hash is what every proof is checked against. Record both to check later that nothing already published has changed. Works on either kind of log - it reads a signed tree head from an RFC 6962 log and a checkpoint from a tiled one - so a workflow does not have to know which it got. No account or API key required.
get_tree_head.name: get_tree_head

parameters.description: Which log to read. This dropdown offers every log the list names, retired and rejected ones included, with the state on each label - a retired log still holds everything it ever held. Typed by hand it takes a log id, a description, or the log's URL.
parameters.name: log

age_seconds.description: How long ago that was; a healthy log signs a fresh one every few minutes. Null for a tiled log

state.description: Its state in the published list

maximum_merge_delay_seconds.description: How long the log may take to include something it accepted

published_at.description: The same moment as ISO 8601, or null

root_hash.description: The Merkle root committing to all of them, base64

root_hash_hex.description: The same root hash in hex

signature.description: The log's signature over the tree head

signature_count.description: How many signatures it carries; a tiled log's checkpoint is also signed by independent witnesses

timestamp.description: When the log signed it, epoch milliseconds; null for a tiled log, whose checkpoint carries no time

tree_size.description: How many entries the log holds

list_log_operators.description: List the organisations that run Certificate Transparency logs - Google, Cloudflare, Let's Encrypt, DigiCert, Sectigo and the rest - with how many logs each runs, how many of those are usable, how they split between the two log formats, and the contact addresses they publish. Useful for spreading monitoring across operators, which is the point of having several. No account or API key required.
list_log_operators.name: list_log_operators

list_logs.description: List the Certificate Transparency logs, from the same published list Chrome itself uses. Each one comes back with who runs it, its URL, its state, whether it speaks the RFC 6962 API or the newer tiled format, and - the part that usually decides which log to read - the window of certificate expiry dates it accepts, because logs are sharded by year. Filter by state, by operator, by kind, or by a word in the name. Start here when a workflow needs to pick a log. No account or API key required.
list_logs.name: list_logs

parameters.description: Only logs in these states. A log's state is what says whether it is worth reading: browsers only trust certificates logged to a usable one, a retired log is frozen, and a rejected one failed qualification and proves nothing. Choose none to see every log.
parameters.name: states

options.label: Usable - trusted, and taking new certificates
Qualified - passed its tests, being included
Pending - has asked to be included
Retired - no longer trusted for new certificates
Unknown - the list gives no state (test and mirror logs)

parameters.description: Only logs run by this organisation. Leave empty for all of them.
parameters.name: operator

parameters.description: Only logs of this kind. RFC 6962 logs answer the original JSON API and are the only ones that serve proofs; tiled logs publish static files instead. Reading tree heads and entries works on either.
parameters.name: log_type

options.label: RFC 6962 - the original API, and serves proofs

parameters.description: Only logs whose name, URL or operator contains this text, matched without regard to case. Leave empty for all of them.
parameters.name: query

parameters.description: What order the logs come back in.
parameters.name: sort_by

options.label: The expiry window the log covers

parameters.description: How many logs to return. The list holds about 120 logs in total, so the default of 50 covers every usable one.
parameters.name: limit

log_list_version.description: The version of the published list read

final_tree_size.description: For a read-only log, the size it was frozen at; else null

description: Read the public Certificate Transparency logs from a workflow. Every publicly trusted certificate on the web has to be published to these append-only logs before a browser will accept it, so they are the one place that can answer what certificates exist for a name and who issued them without asking the certificate authority. Browse the logs Chrome itself trusts and who runs them, work out which one could hold a certificate from its expiry date, read a log's size and root hash, list the CA roots it accepts, and read its newest entries with every certificate decoded into its domain names, issuer and validity - or scan for the ones covering a domain you own, which is how a workflow catches a certificate nobody meant to issue. Ask a log to prove an entry is really in it, or that it has only ever appended, and the proof is checked for you. Works with both the original RFC 6962 logs and the newer tiled ones. Every action reads: nothing here changes anything. No account or API key required.
